What is
the time?
Flying towards the sunrise (i.e., East), one sees the sun earlier than
it would have been seen from the point of departure. In other words,
if you fly East you shorten your hours of daylight, and alternatively,
flying West, you are tending to "keep up with" the sun and so
lengthen your daylight hours.
To keep your watches in synchronisation with the daylight, it is
necessary to make the following corrections:

THE INTERNATIONAL DATE LINE
The International Date Line was created to standardise the com-
mencing and finishing point of a calendar day. Based on the meridian
of 180° from Greenwich, it is an arbitrary line drawn on a map from
North to South.
The effect
of the International Date Line is as
follows: When you cross the I.D.L. on the northbound trip you must
immediately re-commence the 24 hours you have just completed: on
the southbound trip the reverse conditions apply and, on crossing
the I.D.L., a complete day is omitted. (For example, if you cross the
I.D.L. at 3 p.m. flying westward on what you know as Tuesday, the
day immediately becomes 3 p.m. on Wednesday.)
The Story of the
"SOU
ERN CROSS" Route
The "Southern Cross" route,
named
after the first plane to fly the Pacific,
was pioneered in 1928 by Sir Charles
Kingsford Smith, C. P. T. Ulm, H. W
Lyon and J. Warner. On May 31, 1928,
the "Southern Cross" took off from Oak-
land, California, on the first stage of the
record flight to Brisbane, Australia. 27
hours later, Kingsford Smith made a per-
fect landing at Hawaii. As soon as the
"Southern Cross" was refuelled and the crew rested, the second stage,
3,128 trackless miles to Fiji, was begun. Despite instrument trouble,
the "Southern Cross" landed at Fiji 34 hours later. The flight from Fili
to Brisbane was made through tropical storms, necessitating much
instrument flying.
However, on June 9, after a total of 82 hours 42
minutes in the air, the "Southern Cross," the first aircraft to negotiate
the 7,000 miles across the Pacific, touched down at Brisbane.
It is interesting to
compare the performance of the "Southern
Cross" with that of BCPA's DC-6 Airliners.

For the interest and information of passengers, three instru-
ments are situated above the magazine racks, near the cloak-
room.
These are:
CLOCK:
Showing accurate Local Time.
AIRSPEED INDICATOR:
This instrument shows the Indicated Airspeed (I.A.S.) of the
aircraft and is calibrated fo a standard condition of pressure
and temperature.
Variations of these factors,
such as are
experienced at height, necessitate corrections to the I.A.S. to
obtain
the
True Airspeed (T.A.S.).
The
corrections to
be
applied are shown on a scale beside the instrument. As an
example, if the aircraft is flying at 18,000 feet and the I.A.S.
is 220 m.p.h., the T.A.S. of the aircraft is actually 314 m.p.h. at
standard temperature for 18,000 ft., which is 21° C.
I.A.S. and T.A.S. are not to be confused with Ground Speed,
which is the actual speed of the aircraft over the ground. It is
arrived at by taking into consideration wind speed and direc-
tion and then adding or subtracting this component from the
T.A.S.

ALTIMETER:
This instrument is actually a barometer, calibrated to read in
thousands and hundreds of feet and gives the height of the
aircraft above sea level. An additional reading, the "Altitude"
of the pressurised cabin, is shown on this Altimeter. This read-
ing shows the altitude represented by the air pressure inside
the cabin of your "pressurised" airliner.
